title: Jev for NPC AI?
author: keytonw
selftext: Has anyone started looking at Typesafe AI’s Jev for NPC AI? I’ve just started looking at it. Curious if anyone has any experience so far?

comments.author: No-Trouble-9138
comments.body: It's not efficient for dynamic dialogs. It would do better at predefined Q&A, classifying items in an inventory, things like that.

comments.author: EchoingAngel
comments.body: I haven't dug deep enough into it yet, but would it have any place as the "brain" of NPC's for making complex, but somewhat random decisions? I was originally just going to use d20 type rolls for these special agent NPC's to mimic player actions

replies.author: codeninja
replies.body:
Yes, I've been tinkering with battle Sims and jev is efficient at selecting the right options to lead to an objective. 

Im defining world state and action state, along with appropriate rules and decision drivers in The request and letting jev drive lots of different scenarios.

replies.author: Sebguer
replies.body: It's basically a classifier engine, so it can only return probabilities across set number of enums. But, if you can boil down your decisions to that, it could be useful. It's quite dumb, though, so I'm not sure how well it would handle actual complexity. I think the current hype is kind of overblown, but the premise is really strong and it put more attention on it, so I'd expect some much stronger versions to emerge soon.

replies.author: EchoingAngel
replies.body: Sounds perfect for NPC "agents" in a wider world that can approximate the best next action. The goal is for them to act unpredictable, but sensibly, and only use data they are exposed to

replies.body: I've been thinking of doing the same but I haven't fully wrapped my brain around it yet

comments.author: Flannakis
comments.body: I have played around with jev and 2 basic 3d avatars, that react to a first persons actions. It’s very responsive, but I see it more for reflex type actions, ie a player raise their hand to strike and the jev ai may cower, maybe the thinking:reasoning remains LLMs whilst actions/reflexes are jev? Keen to hear how others are using

comments.author: Jolly-Rip5973
comments.body:
Jev isn't a text generation model.   
It can only pick from a list of preset things. 

It doesn't necessarily always pick the best thing either. 

If you really want NPC behavior your would probably just use deterministic code, create some need meters that drop over time, like hunger, tiredness, loneliness, etc. and then match up a behavior to the needs gauges, just like the Sims. 

Alternative put the NPCs of scheduling system like Elder Scrolls Oblivion. 

just because he have AI models doesn't mean they are always the best option when deterministic code is like 100s of time more efficient and predictable.   
  
Adding some type of small LLM to give the NPCs the ability to chat with each other would make the world seem a little more alive.

replies.author: EchoingAngel
replies.body: But what if the point is more realistic NPCs that can generally pick predictable things, but they vary over time and can eventually go rogue? Not even necessarily for all your NPCs, but special "agents" that are wildcards in sim games

replies.author: Jolly-Rip5973
replies.body:
What going to make you NPCs human like or realistic is some type of needs so they have to eat, drink, poop, pee, sleep, work, etc. 

The sims is called the sims because they are Simulated People. 

The sim's need system was based on Maslow's Hierarchy of needs. 

The original Oblivion NPC AI was very sophisticated and NPCs could go rogue and do quite interesting things, They had to dumb it down though because the NPCs would break the game. Like one NPC might cheat on another NPCs wife and then the husband find out and attacks him, but the NPC gets killed but he was a quest giver, so now the quest system is broken. 

Eventually they had to make all NPCs related to quest unkillable. 

There a video I watched on YouTube explaining the Oblivion NPC system. Even dumbed down, it more sophisticated the modern games like Red Dead Redemption or cyberpunk or the Witcher. 

Game was really ahead of it's time. Most sophisticated NPC system is probably Dwarf Fortress. 

Anyhoo, you have to somehow balance out making your NPCs seem autonomous without breaking the world or the questing system. 

There have been some experiments using ChatGPT and Claude to run NPCs villages but they always end up killing each other in two or three days. It never ends wells. 

You don't actually need to have true AI NPCs though, you just need to create an illusion of autonomy and an interconnected world.

comments.author: tomqmasters
comments.body: whatever you are feeding into JEV as a criteria for better or worse decision making can almost certainly be used in a regular action planning system.

comments.author: Sisyph_328
comments.body:
I caught a livestream in their Discord the other day where they had Jev control a character to test a platformer. It was making decisions really fast, almost as fast as a person reacting. A coworker recently tried it with Codex too and said it cut token usage a lot.

I like your idea of using it for NPC AI. I hadn’t thought of that before you brought it up.

My main worry is that the NPCs might make every decision too quickly or go straight for the obvious choice. You’d probably need something to control when they act, give them a moment to hesitate sometimes. Just those little moments where they don’t seem completely sure what to do. That’s part of what makes interacting with them feel natural.

replies.author: EchoingAngel
replies.body: I feel like there would be a way to poison or sandbag their data intentionally, or we just combine their decision making with RNG to pick the top # prediction. Then difficulty could just be reducing the count on the "dice" so better predictions are more and more likely (easy is 1-10, medium is 1-6, hard is 1-3)

replies.author: Sisyph_328
replies.body: I agree, a dice roll could work. I was thinking different NPCs could have different flaws in how they make decisions. A reckless one might stay in a fight too long, a timid one might retreat too early. Those tendencies could be baked into the randomness.
